cards.title: Where did it go?
cards.body:
You press **Save** and your essay disappears from the screen. But where did it actually go?

It became a **file** in [[storage]], filed away by the [[operating system]] so you (and your apps) can find it again.

cards.title: Files, folders and extensions
cards.body:
A **file** is one named piece of saved data: a photo, a song, an essay or an app.

Files go in **folders**, and folders can hold other folders, like boxes inside boxes. The route through the boxes to a file is its **path**: `Documents > School > essay.docx`.

The end of a file's name, after the last dot, is its **extension**. It tells the OS what kind of file it is and which app should open it: `.jpg` and `.png` are pictures, `.mp3` a song, `.mp4` a video, `.docx` a document (with styles like bold and headings) and `.txt` plain text (just letters, no styles). `.exe` is a **program**: opening it runs it.

cards.prompt: Match each [[extension]] to the kind of file it marks.

pairs.right: A program that runs when opened

cards.explanation: `.jpg` is a photo, `.mp3` a song, `.mp4` a video and `.docx` a document. `.exe` is different: it's a **program**. Opening it *runs* it, so only open ones you trust.
cards.hint: The extension tells the OS what kind of file it is. Think back to the list: pictures, songs, videos, documents and programs.
cards.nudge: Look again at the letters: `.mp3` and `.mp4` look alike but mark different things, and one extension means a program.

cards.prompt: Label what each file really is. Read to the **last** dot.
cards.explanation: `photo.jpg.exe` ends in **.exe**, so it's a program, whatever the `.jpg` in the middle says. `notes.txt` is plain text: just letters, with no styles like bold or headings.
cards.hint: Read each file name right to the end. Only the [[extension]] after the **last** dot counts.
cards.nudge: A name can have more than one dot. Ignore anything in the middle and look only at what comes after the last dot.

cards.title: The cloud
cards.body:
Not every file lives on your device. When you save to **the cloud**, the file is stored on a company's **server**: a powerful computer in a data centre, reached over the internet.

The cloud isn't in the sky. It's someone else's computer, usually kept safe and [[backed up|backup]].

Cloud files are handy: you can open them on any device and they survive if your phone is lost. But you need the internet to reach them, unless you've kept a copy on the device.

cards.prompt: Where is each file stored: **on your device** or **in the cloud**?

items.label: A song downloaded to play offline
A drawing saved to the laptop's storage
A shared doc you edit in a web browser
Emails in a web mail inbox
A game save kept in your online account

cards.explanation: Files you **downloaded** or **saved to the device** are in its storage. Files you reach through a **website or online account** live on the company's servers, in the cloud.
cards.hint: Ask yourself: did you download or save it to the device, or do you reach it through a website or online account?
cards.nudge: Files downloaded or saved to the device live in its storage. Files you reach through a website or account live on a company's [[server]].

cards.prompt: A website promised free holiday wallpapers. You clicked download.

steps.text: Your Downloads folder now has a new file: `photo.jpg.exe`. What is it?

choices.consequence: Only the **last** [[extension]] counts. The `.jpg` in the middle is a disguise.

choices.text: A program pretending to be a photo
choices.consequence: Right. It ends in **.exe**, so opening it would run it.

steps.text: What do you do with it?

choices.text: Open it once, just to check
choices.consequence: Opening a program runs it, and it only takes one run for it to do harm.

choices.text: Send it to a friend to try
choices.consequence: Now your friend's device is at risk too. Never pass on a file you don't trust.

choices.text: Delete it without opening it, and tell an adult
choices.consequence: The file is gone, and an adult can check nothing else came with it.

cards.explanation: Read to the **last** dot. `photo.jpg.exe` is a program in disguise. Some computers hide the last extension, so it might even show as `photo.jpg`. Delete files like this without opening them, and tell an adult.
cards.hint: Read the file name right to the last dot. What does that extension mean happens when you open it?

cards.prompt: Your science essay is saved inside these folders. Put its path in order, from the **biggest folder** (the one holding everything else) to the file.
cards.explanation: A path goes from the biggest box inwards: `Documents > School > Science > volcanoes.docx`. The file itself always comes last.
cards.hint: Think of boxes inside boxes: start with the biggest box that holds everything, then go inwards.
cards.nudge: A path goes from the biggest folder inwards, one box at a time. The file itself always comes last.

cards.prompt: Each photo you take is about **4 [[MB|megabyte]]**. There are **1,000 MB** in 1 [[GB|gigabyte]]. How many photos fit in **1 GB**?
cards.hint: Divide 1,000 MB by the size of one photo.
cards.explanation: 1,000 ÷ 4 = **250** photos in every gigabyte. So a phone with 64 GB free could hold about 16,000 of them.
cards.nudge: Check you divided rather than multiplied: how many 4 MB photos fit into 1,000 MB?

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- A **file** is saved data with a name. **Folders** hold files and other folders, and the route to a file is its **path**.
- The **extension** after the last dot says what kind of file it is. `.exe` means a program.
- **Cloud** files live on a company's [[servers|server]], reached over the internet.
- A name like `photo.jpg.exe` is a program in disguise: delete it and tell an adult.

That's the software side. Next module: fixing things yourself.
